claims: The authors estimate brand-choice models on household buying data to distinguish state dependence from persistent heterogeneity, search, and learning.
The study explains repeat brand purchases and compares search to other mechanisms of consumer inertia.

locator: Hierarchical Choice Model and Dynamic Category Pricing
claims: A hierarchical brand-choice model fits household purchase data and allows loyalty to change the utility of a brand.
The authors solve a retailer's dynamic pricing problem and compare optimal prices with and without model-implied loyalty.
The authors learn individualized pricing from a randomized pricing field experiment and validate the prices in the field.
Simulations compare profits and consumer welfare across levels of personalization and data granularity.
The paper estimates a tobacco demand model with household heterogeneity and addiction using observed sales and television advertising.
The estimated demand model is used to simulate the effect of a proposed ban on e-cigarette television advertising.

locator: Abstract, experimental design and online appendix
claims: Participants recruited through Mechanical Turk received different ad content in a controlled online bookstore environment created by the authors.
The study tracks how what an ad reveals changes the books a consumer searches for.

locator: Abstract and Study Design and Measurement Approach
claims: Fifteen randomized Facebook advertising experiments provide benchmarks for testing observational estimates of campaign lift.
The paper benchmarks double/debiased machine learning and propensity-score matching against experimental estimates. The nonexperimental approaches do not reliably recover the causal effect.
The benchmarks come from 663 large Facebook field experiments on actual ad campaigns.
The authors model equilibrium advertising and price competition when advertising shifts preferences between rival brands.
A laboratory experiment studies how competing advertisements change brand preferences.
A principal–agent model embedded in a differentiated duopoly derives implications of personalized price and quality offers.
In Study 1, gym users followed instructions emphasizing immediate or delayed rewards and their actual workout persistence was recorded.
Study 1 relates the content of New York Times articles to naturally observed sharing.
In Studies 2a–2c, random assignment to story variants varying in emotional arousal tests their effect on reported sharing intentions.
The paper uses computer vision and deep learning on in-store video to predict purchase decisions.
A regional intervention and synthetic difference-in-differences estimate how TV advertising changes browsing and sales over time.
The outcomes come from an online travel platform and are linked to TV campaign exposure.
Two deep neural networks are integrated into a difference-in-differences model to estimate heterogeneous effects in matched creator data.
The application selects creators for a signing program at a video-sharing platform.
A profit-weighted loss ranks customers by projected gains from retention offers.
Two field experiments compare profitability of retention campaigns built by the proposed model and its alternatives.
A field experiment on WeChat and three controlled online studies vary displayed likes and measure responses to social ads.
A Facebook Ads field experiment and separate laboratory and online experiments vary the speed of clips to test viewers’ responses.
